Joshua W.J. Brown

How Sloppy Reporting Made Ceuta’s Migration Story Worse

Share on Facebook
Tweet
Share on LinkedIn
Share this article by email
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:21
Instaread

The most dangerous sentence in a migration crisis is the one that removes the victim.

That is what bothered me about some of the reporting and social-media commentary surrounding sexual assaults in Ceuta after the July 30 mass crossing. A headline can say that sexual assaults are rising after tens of thousands of migrants arrived and be technically tethered to a real concern. But if it does not tell readers who the victims are, it can create an entirely different story in their minds.

The available evidence is more complicated. Reuters reported on August 18 that Spain’s largest police union, SUP, said 15 sexual assaults of varying severity had been reported in Ceuta since July 30, and that a significant majority of the victims were minors. Reuters also reported that Spain’s National Police and Interior Ministry declined to confirm the union’s total. Three days later, Human Rights Watch reported that Ceuta’s public prosecutor’s office had received 13 sexual-assault cases between July 30 and August 17, with most victims not resident in the city.

Those figures should not be collapsed into a single statistic. A police-union count, a prosecutor’s caseload, a health-service tally, and a set of court proceedings represent different forms of evidence. Good reporting keeps the source and status attached to every number.

Then comes the detail that changes the frame. By August 12, Ceuta’s judicial authorities had processed three sexual-assault cases involving migrant women who were allegedly assaulted by Moroccan migrants arriving during the mass influx. Two of the victims were minors. In other words, some of the clearest court-documented victims were migrants themselves.

Reuters also interviewed women sleeping near the overcrowded reception centre who described harassment and fear of assault by men around the improvised camps. Human-rights organisations warned that migrant women and girls were extremely vulnerable because of unsafe sleeping arrangements, inadequate privacy, and insufficient protected accommodation.

There was also a separate case involving a local Ceuta woman. A migrant entered a private home and climbed into her bed in his underwear. A judge ordered his deportation on a breaking-and-entering charge. That is serious. It is also not the same as saying that the confirmed sexual-assault cases primarily involved local Spanish girls attacked by newly arrived migrants.

This distinction should be basic journalism. It is not political correctness. It is subject, verb, and object.

Who was assaulted? Who is accused? Which authority confirmed the case? Which number represents an allegation, which a union estimate, and which a court proceeding? If those questions disappear, the audience is left to fill in the gaps with whatever story it already expects to be true.

Migration stories are particularly vulnerable to this distortion because scale itself creates fear. At least 72,000 people crossed into a city of about 84,000 residents on July 30. Most were young men, and by August 28, Reuters reported that roughly 5,000 to 8,000 people remained in Ceuta. The visual impression was enormous. Once that image takes hold, a loosely written crime headline can convert population shock into collective suspicion almost instantly.

That is unfair to local residents with legitimate security concerns, because exaggerated claims are easy to discredit and can make real problems harder to discuss. It is also unfair to migrant women and girls, because those most vulnerable to sexual violence can disappear inside a narrative that presents migrants only as the source of danger.

Both groups deserve better than propaganda.

Ceuta does have a real safety problem. The reception centre was over capacity. Women were sleeping outside beside men they did not know. Police and social services were scrambling. Spain’s health minister said five women had received medical treatment for sexual violence; Human Rights Watch later reported that four emergency-room doctors said they had treated two women and six girls for sexual assault or rape. Courts and prosecutors were processing cases. None of this is a reason to minimise the crisis.

They are reasons to describe it accurately.

Accuracy also changes the policy response. If the problem is framed primarily as foreign men attacking local girls, the obvious response becomes more policing of migrants. If the evidence shows that migrant women and girls are also among the principal victims, then protected accommodation, gender-separated sanitation, child protection, lighting, staffed shelters, and rapid registration become security measures too.

A distorted story therefore does not merely produce distorted public opinion. It can produce the wrong operational response.

This is especially important when a figure such as “15 sexual assaults” begins circulating. The responsible response is not to suppress it, but to keep its status attached: SUP said 15 assaults had been reported; Reuters reported that the National Police and Interior Ministry declined to confirm the union’s total; Ceuta prosecutors later told Human Rights Watch they had received 13 sexual-assault cases through August 17; courts had already processed specific cases; and several of the clearest court-documented victims were migrants. Different numbers can all be accurate while answering different questions.

That takes more words than a viral headline. Reality usually does.

I do not think the public needs to be protected from ugly facts about crimes committed during migration crises. I think the public needs those ugly facts in the correct order. Ceuta is serious enough without inventing a simpler version of it.

Patricia Zanini Graca

Women Who Refuse to Be Victims

Share on Facebook
Tweet
Share on LinkedIn
Share this article by email

For years, I avoided stories about women like me—women who had endured psychological and physical violence. It was not because I doubted the importance of telling them. Quite the opposite. Stories about domestic abuse, coercive control, and the quiet devastation that unfolds behind closed doors need to be told. They illuminate realities that too often remain hidden or misunderstood.

But some stories live in the body long after the mind has tried to leave them behind. A scene, a sentence, a look—and suddenly, you are no longer watching a film or reading a book. You are back there. So when I began watching Furious, I fully expected to switch it off. To my surprise, I did not.

Something about the series compelled me to stay. Perhaps it was because, for once, the women on screen were not simply enduring violence. They were not permanently confined to the role of victim. They were taking ownership of their stories and shaping what came next. That distinction matters more than we often acknowledge.

Furious is aptly named. Female rage runs through every episode like an electric current. Yet this is not the familiar version of rage popular culture has historically assigned to women—the kind that must eventually be punished, softened, redeemed, or explained away. Here, anger is not treated as a character defect requiring correction. Instead, the series asks a more unsettling question: What happens when women stop accepting the rules written for them?

The series follows three remarkable women, portrayed by Emmy Rossum, Lola Petticrew, and Quincy Tyler Bernstine, whose lives intersect through violence, crime, trauma, and institutional failure. On the surface, it offers every ingredient of a gripping thriller: a serial killer, a detective, a sex-trafficking investigation, and enough darkness to satisfy any devotee of the genre. Beneath the suspense, however, lies something more profound.

Furious is fundamentally interested in what trauma does to women and, perhaps more important, what women choose to do with it. That question landed harder than I expected.

I know what it means to leave in order to survive. I also know that courage does not always look like standing your ground. Sometimes it looks like walking away. Sometimes it means packing fragments of your life into a suitcase and stepping into uncertainty because staying has become unbearable. I ran because I needed to survive. I did not seek revenge. That distinction, too, matters.

Our cultural narratives too often suggest that women who experience abuse are left with only two choices: forgive their abusers and move serenely forward, or surrender to anger and vengeance. As though these were the only endings available. They are not. There is another path—the path of reinvention.

It belongs to the woman who leaves and gradually realizes that the person she spent years trying to become was shaped by fear, manipulation, or someone else’s expectations. She learns to trust herself again. She stops apologizing for taking up space. She finds her voice after years of silence. Most of all, she understands that surviving was never the final chapter. It was only the beginning.

That is what made Furious unexpectedly liberating for me. I was not merely watching women suffer. I was watching them interpret their experiences, make choices, reclaim agency, and, in some cases, seize power. I was watching women become the protagonists of their own lives. And I realized how hungry I was for stories like theirs.

For generations, women have been extraordinarily well represented as victims. On screen, we have been beaten, violated, murdered, abandoned, betrayed, manipulated, and traumatized in every imaginable way. Our suffering has been photographed, dramatized, romanticized, and packaged for public consumption.

Too often, the violence becomes the spectacle while the woman herself recedes from view, reduced to a wound, a warning, or a device in someone else’s story. We know what female pain looks like; we have seen it countless times. What we encounter far less often is what comes after.

Where are the stories about the woman who leaves and builds a life she loves? The woman who turns her wounds into wisdom? The woman who succeeds not because trauma somehow improved her, but because she refused to let it define the limits of her future? Where is the woman whose story does not end when the violence does? That, after all, is the story many women are actually living.

Most survivors do not spend the rest of their lives trapped inside the moment that wounded them. They rebuild careers, raise children, fall in love again, start businesses, take risks, earn degrees, become leaders, and rediscover joy. They live. Yet these stories remain strangely absent from our cultural imagination.

Perhaps resilience is considered less dramatic than suffering. Perhaps female empowerment still makes people uncomfortable. Or perhaps a woman who refuses to remain a victim challenges assumptions that society has not yet learned to discard. Whatever the reason, we need more narratives willing to move beyond survival. Stories about pain remain essential, but survival deserves a sequel.

It is time to stop asking women to make their anger palatable. Let women be furious. Let them be ambitious, complicated, brilliant, messy, sexual, powerful, and imperfect. Let them make mistakes. Let them fail and begin again. Let them occupy space without apology and tell the truth without immediately being asked whether their pain is justified or their anger reasonable. Most important, let them tell us what happened next. Women have been surviving chaos for centuries.

The truly radical story now is not about how women endure suffering. It is about what happens when they emerge from it—not merely alive, healed, or grateful, but thriving.

The journey from chaos to power is neither simple nor linear. It is messy, painful, and often deeply uncomfortable. Yet it is worth portraying because it reminds us that resilience is not resignation, and survival is not the same as living. For too long, women have been handed endings written by others. Perhaps it is time we wrote our own. This time, we get to decide how the story ends.

Binoy Kampmark

Thieving Matters: The Trump-Venezuela Oil Steal

Share on Facebook
Tweet
Share on LinkedIn
Share this article by email

When the Trump administration abducted the Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife on January 3, an open incitement to international lawbreaking was asserted. Here was thuggish impunity, crude acquisition, and harsh plunder in operation: the seizure of a sovereign leader in office on fanciful narco-terrorist charges, a violation of the territorial sanctity of a state guaranteed by Article 2 of the United Nations Charter, and the demand that Venezuela be compliant with Washington’s objectives in its vulgar reiteration of the Monroe Doctrine. The prize was clearly oil.

Towards the end of August, President Donald Trump was in a sprightly mood on his favourite platform of choice, Truth Social. In a post, the president announced that he had reached, with Venezuela, “THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!” Under his direction, the U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, working with interim President Delcy Rodriguez of Venezuela in “partnership with private business, have secured majority U.S. control of more than 65 BILLION BARRELS of proven Oil Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the American taxpayer.”

This brazen assertion of control would more than double oil reserves in the U.S. (currently at 46 billion barrels), increase oil supply and, most importantly regarding the election prospects for the Republicans, “substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans, long into the future, while helping to continue to set Venezuela on a course to Tremendous Success and Great Prosperity.”

President Rodriguez tried to polish what could only be regarded as a particularly unpleasant turd. Lasting 25 years, the agreement was in line with the country’s Hydrocarbons Law and would secure $100 billion in investment, with $209.3 billion in royalties and taxes. She was less than forthcoming about the level of tax revenue that will flow in from these transactions.

This cocksure initiative is, as with much issuing from the mind and easy mouth of Trump, one part hope and several parts fiction. The initial question to ask is when the benefits of this plunderous exercise will flow back to the American economy in any timely way. “Ultimately, prices are going to come down,” Trump remarked in the Oval Office. “Now, will it happen before the election? I can’t tell you that.”

The cognoscenti in the field of commodities are sceptical and excited. Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, offered his doubts to The Hill. Well, it might be that prices would come down “several years from now,” but that was hardly likely in the short term. There were, for instance, troubling legal risks to the agreement, and various other contingencies, but were it to have legs, “with huge investments, with a big increase in oil production, it could be big. But, again, the gas price impacts are years down the road, not days, weeks or months.”

These comments easily inspire reference to those damning words of the economist John Maynard Keynes, penned in A Tract of Monetary Reform (1923): “The long run is a misleading guide to current affairs. In the long run we are all dead.” Gas prices might fall, but in the short term, we have Trump’s airy, often buffoonish assessments.

There are a multitude of considerations as to why the long run matters. From Lipow Oil Associates, Andy Lipow reminds us about the necessary infrastructure for the venture to work. “It’s going to take a decade to upgrade the infrastructure system to have a material impact on the oil market,” though he did not wish to ignore the possibility of “some incremental improvements in the next year or two.” To push Venezuelan oil to levels of high production could cost somewhere in the order of $180 billion; “an extraordinary amount of money [is needed] to be spent just to get oil out of the ground and delivered to the market before it’s even refined.”

The agreement has all the crude tailoring of gangster capitalism. The Trump administration is not exactly forthcoming on the list of enlisted business partners, but one reliably soiled candidate is North American Blue Energy partners (NABEP), led by the Venezuelan investor Alejandro Betancourt. The company is planning to move six drilling rigs into its Venezuelan oil fields by the end of the year, with the intention of deploying a further 12 rigs in 2027. The anticipated total is 52.

In keeping with Trump’s taste for squalid, thieving characters, Betancourt is under investigation for overseeing the embezzling of $2 billion from state oil company Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), having also caught the eye of authorities in Spain and Switzerland for alleged money laundering and tax fraud. Despite this seemingly choking cloud of suspicion and query, Betancourt has been given near complete freedom to use private planes, accompanied by his troupe of family, partners, investors, and business associates from the banking and mining industries.

As for the aforementioned legal risks, these are hard to shake off. Does the transaction pass muster under the Venezuelan constitution, given that Washington, not Caracas, is the one deciding the model at stake and companies that will participate in the venture? Trump has no care in the world for such statutory niceties, but prospective business partners and investors do. Luisa Palacios, an adjunct researcher at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, is blunt on this point: “If the goal was to try to reduce the risk of investing in Venezuela, the United States might be doing the exact opposite with this transaction: further weakening the country’s already fragile institutional framework.”

Ed Chow, former Chevron executive and non-resident senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, has this to add: “For a capital intensive, long-term industry, uncertainty slows you down. Sometimes it freezes you.” If there is a freeze in all of this, it certainly will not be due to any moral scruples on the part of the parties. However rich the returns, Venezuelan clientelism and kleptocratic initiative has been assured.
